analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar sitting members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, and derivative-style instruments. Lawmakers could still invest through diversified mutual funds and ETFs, the federal retirement plan, or Treasury securities, and could use a qualified blind trust. Any profit from a prohibited trade would go back to the Treasury, losses could not be written off on taxes, and each member would have to certify compliance every year for publication online, with audits at least every two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who cannot trade on early knowledge of legislation and agency decisions would gain a level field, and the market overall would benefit from less appearance of congressional self-dealing. Members who honestly avoid conflicts would gain a clearer rule.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual securities, security futures, commodities, and synthetic-derivative positions during their terms of service.
Allows continued investing only through diversified mutual funds and ETFs, the Thrift Savings Plan, and Treasury securities, or through a qualified blind trust.
Requires profits from prohibited trades to be disgorged to the Treasury, bars deducting losses from prohibited trades against income tax, and exposes violators to civil fines.
Requires each member to certify compliance annually to the supervising ethics office, which must publish the certifications online and audit members' compliance at least every two years.
For current members, the ban would have applied starting on the first day of the second session of the 118th Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to move individual stocks into diversified funds or blind trusts and give up the ability to pick individual investments while in office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Members and spouses lose the ability to hold individual investments, even where the investment has no plausible connection to their work; blind trusts and diversified funds are the only escape, and blind trusts can be costly to set up and maintain.

Enforcement leans heavily on self-certification and a periodic audit, so a member determined to circumvent the ban through a spouse's accounts or unreported derivatives might be hard to catch in practice.
The bill does not change the existing civil fine schedule for violations, so penalties beyond disgorgement may remain modest relative to the trading profits possible on a member's salary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on a small, financially sophisticated group — sitting lawmakers and their spouses — while the benefit is a clearer rule against trading on information about laws and policy that only members get early. The main design weakness is reliance on self-certification with modest penalties, which would leave room for evasion, but the core ban is straightforward and the exemptions (index funds, TSP, Treasuries) leave plenty of room for normal investing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 21, 2023 by Rep. Zachary Nunn of Iowa, joined by Rep. Stanton, and referred that same day to the House Administration Committee and, in part, to the Ways and Means Committee.
Five other representatives cosponsored the bill — three Democrats and two Republicans — making the initial support bipartisan but small.

No further action appears in the bill's history: neither committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup was scheduled, and the bill never reached a House floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and their spouses are better off, because nothing in current law stops them from holding and trading individual stocks while in office; the bill died without any committee action at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would ban them from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and derivatives during their terms, and claw back profits from violations. Members' own chamber control decided its fate: no committee ever acted on it.

Congressional members would shift individual stock activity into diversified funds, TSP, and Treasury securities, reducing some high-profile individual trading by a small client set. The effect on the industry overall is minor.

industries.industry: Financial market participants and retail investors
industries.note: Removing congressional insider trading (or its appearance) reduces a form of market unfairness that ordinary investors cannot match, since they lack early access to legislative and agency information.
